passage:
A school installed smart boards, tablets, and automatic attendance systems. Visitors praised the modern classrooms.
After one semester, teachers reviewed the results. Some lessons improved. Students could see videos, answer polls, and save notes. But in some classes, the technology distracted more than it helped.
The school decided that every tool needed a learning purpose. A screen should not be used just because it was available.
Students appreciated the change. Lessons became clearer.
The smart classroom became truly smarter when teachers stopped asking, "What can this device do?" and began asking, "What do students need to understand?"
